excerpt: What a personal injury demand letter contains, when your attorney sends one, and how insurers typically respond to it.
keyTakeaways: A personal injury demand letter is a formal document your attorney sends to the insurance company outlining liability, itemizing damages, and demanding compensation. Send after reaching MMI but before the statute of limitations expires (2 years GA, 3 years SC). In Georgia motor-vehicle cases an attorney's pre-suit demand must follow O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1 (at least 30 days to accept, 40 to pay). Bad-faith penalties in both states run against your own insurer only: Georgia's O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6 after a 60-day demand, South Carolina's S.C. Code § 38-59-40 after a 90-day demand. South Carolina has no demand statute for claims against the other driver's insurer.

faqs.question: What is a personal injury demand letter?
faqs.answer: A demand letter is a formal document sent by your attorney to the at-fault party's insurance company. It outlines the facts of the accident, establishes liability, itemizes your damages, and demands a specific amount of compensation.

faqs.question: When should a demand letter be sent?
faqs.answer: After you reach maximum medical improvement (MMI). Georgia's 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina's 3-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) set the outer boundaries.

faqs.question: What should be included in a demand letter?
faqs.answer: A factual narrative, liability argument, itemized economic damages, non-economic damages description, supporting evidence, a specific dollar demand, and a response deadline. In Georgia motor-vehicle cases it must also state the release terms and the 30-day acceptance and 40-day payment dates O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1 requires.

faqs.question: Does Georgia require a demand letter before filing a lawsuit?
faqs.answer: For standard PI claims, no. When a lawyer sends a demand in a motor-vehicle case it must follow O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1. Georgia's bad-faith penalty statute (O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6) requires a 60-day demand and applies only to a claim on your own policy. Government claims require ante litem notice — six months for a city under O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5, and 12 months for a county (§ 36-11-1) or the state (§ 50-21-26).

faqs.question: What happens after the insurance company receives the demand?
faqs.answer: The insurer will accept (rare), counteroffer (most common), reject, or ignore the demand. If negotiations stall, your attorney can file a lawsuit.

faqs.question: Can I write my own demand letter?
faqs.answer: You can, but it is not recommended. A poorly drafted demand that undervalues your claim or admits fault can permanently damage your recovery. An experienced attorney maximizes the demand and anticipates insurer tactics. In Georgia, only a demand prepared with a lawyer's help is an O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1 offer.
